title: Work and careers
cando: talk about your experience and skills, and handle a job interview

about.text: In this lesson you talk about your work, your experience and your skills. You practise a job interview: you answer questions with real examples, and you ask a good question at the end. You also read a job application, and you write a short CV profile and a covering message.
goals: Talk about your experience: I was responsible for …, I'm in charge of …
Answer an interview question with a real example.
Describe results with numbers: twice as many, by far the most.
Read a job application, and write a CV profile and a covering message.
Ask a good question at the end of an interview.

chapters.title: A job interview
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you talk about your work and your skills, and you practise a job interview.
First, you listen to Carlos. He works in a small hotel, and he wants a better job. He has an interview for the position of front office supervisor.
Listen to the questions. The interviewer says: Tell me about a time when you had to work under pressure. This question wants a real example, not an opinion. So Carlos tells a short story: what happened, what he did, and the result.
Listen to how he talks about his job: I was responsible for training new staff. I'm in charge of the weekend team.
At the end, the interviewer asks: Do you have any questions for us? Carlos has a good question ready. Always have one.

chapters.title: The company I worked for
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points in this lesson.
The first is about small words like for, to and of. We say: the company I worked for. The manager I reported to. The small word goes at the end, and we don't need who or which.
Two phrases are very useful at work: responsible for, and in charge of. I was responsible for the stockroom. She's in charge of a team of six. After for and of, use a noun or an -ing word: responsible for training new staff.
The second point is about numbers. Interviewers remember numbers, so say how big the difference was. We had twice as many customers as last year. We had half as many complaints. It was by far the busiest week of the year.

chapters.title: You on paper
chapters.text:
Next, you read a job application. Amina works in customer service, and she wants to be a team leader.
Look at the parts: her profile, her experience, her education and her covering letter.
Her profile is short, and it has numbers in it. She doesn't just say: I'm hard-working. She says what she does, and what she has achieved.
Then you write your own short CV profile, and a covering message for a job you would like.

chapters.title: Your interview
chapters.text:
Then you have a job interview. The interviewer asks you three questions.
Answer each one with a real example. Say what the situation was, what you did, and what the result was. Use a number if you can.
At the end, ask one good question about the job. For example: What would you like the new person to achieve in the first three months?

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Finally, you read a story or an article about work and careers.
Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions.
Think about what the people in it are good at, and what they learn.

warmup.prompt: What is the hardest part of a job interview for you?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Most people feel nervous at an interview. Good preparation helps: before you go, think of real examples from your work.

conversation.title: The interview
conversation.setting: Carlos works as a receptionist at a small hotel. He has an interview at Brookfield Hotels for the position of front office supervisor. Ms Novak, the manager, is interviewing him.
lines: Thanks for coming in, Carlos. So, why did you apply for this position?
I've worked in hotels for six years, and I'd like more responsibility. The hotel I work for now is quite small, so there's no chance of promotion.
I see. And what are you responsible for at the moment?
I'm a receptionist, but I'm also in charge of the weekend team. Last year, I was responsible for training three new staff.
Good. Tell me about a time when you had to work under pressure.
Last August, two receptionists were off sick in the same week, and it was by far the busiest week of the year. We had twice as many guests as usual.
I changed the rota, I asked a colleague from the restaurant to help, and I worked two extra shifts. We didn't get a single complaint.
That's impressive. What would you say is your biggest weakness?
I find it hard to say no, so I sometimes take on too much. Now I'm learning to share the work.
Thank you. Do you have any questions for us?
Yes. What would you like the new supervisor to achieve in the first three months?
Good question. Mainly faster check-ins. Our target is three minutes for each guest. We'll let you know by Friday.
Thank you. I look forward to hearing from you.

questions.q: What is Carlos in charge of at the moment?
questions.why: Carlos says: I'm also in charge of the weekend team.

questions.q: Why was that week in August difficult?
questions.a: Two receptionists were off sick, and the hotel was very busy.
questions.why: Two receptionists were off sick, and there were twice as many guests as usual.

questions.q: What does Carlos ask at the end?
questions.a: what the new supervisor should achieve in the first three months
wrong: when he can start the job
questions.why: He asks: What would you like the new supervisor to achieve in the first three months?

phrases.text: Tell me about a time when you had to work under pressure.
phrases.use: An interview question that asks for a real example.

phrases.text: I was responsible for training new staff.
I'm in charge of the weekend team.
phrases.use: Saying which people or which work you manage.

phrases.text: We had twice as many guests as usual.
phrases.use: Giving a result with a number.

phrases.text: I find it hard to say no, but I'm learning to share the work.
Do you have any questions for us?
phrases.use: The interviewer asks this at the end. Always have a question ready.

phrases.text: I look forward to hearing from you.
phrases.use: A polite way to end an interview or a letter.

items.meaning: A job in a company or an organisation.
items.example: I'm applying for the position of shift supervisor.

items.meaning: A job that is available because nobody is doing it at the moment.
items.example: There's a vacancy for a driver at the warehouse.

items.meaning: A person who is trying to get a job, for example at an interview.
items.example: They're interviewing five candidates for the job.

items.meaning: Something that you are good at, or a good quality that you have.
items.example: My main strength is dealing with difficult customers.

items.meaning: Something that you are not so good at, or a quality that you want to improve.
items.example: My weakness is that I find it hard to say no.

items.meaning: Having skills and knowledge because you have done a job or an activity for a long time.
items.example: We're looking for an experienced chef.

items.meaning: Wanting to do something well, and ready to work hard for it.
items.example: The new staff are very motivated, and they learn fast.

items.meaning: Arriving or doing something at the right time, not late.
items.example: Please be punctual. The shift starts at six.

items.meaning: Good at thinking of new ideas, or new ways of doing things.
items.example: She found a creative way to cut our costs.

items.meaning: Able to change your plans or your hours easily when it is necessary.
items.example: I'm flexible, so I can work evenings and weekends.

items.meaning: When people work well together to do a job.
items.example: Good teamwork is very important in a busy kitchen.

items.meaning: In a difficult situation, with a lot of work or very little time.
items.example: Can you work well under pressure?

items.meaning: To succeed in doing something, usually after working hard.
items.example: We achieved all our sales targets last year.

items.meaning: A result or a number that you try to reach.
items.example: Our target is fifty new customers a month.

items.meaning: The opinion or feeling that you get about someone, especially when you first meet them.
items.example: He made a very good impression at the interview.

sound.title: Word stress: punctual, experienced
sound.explain: In a long word, one part is stronger than the others. Punctual, flexible and motivated have the stress on the first part: PUNC-tual, FLEX-ible, MO-tivated. Experienced, creative and reliable have it on the second part: ex-PE-rienced, cre-A-tive, re-LI-able. Listen, then say each group.

sayIt.instructions: Say Carlos's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you sound calm and clear, like a strong candidate?
lines: I'm a receptionist, but I'm also in charge of the weekend team. Last year, I was responsible for training three new staff.
Last August, two receptionists were off sick in the same week, and it was by far the busiest week of the year. We had twice as many guests as usual.
I changed the rota, I asked a colleague from the restaurant to help, and I worked two extra shifts. We didn't get a single complaint.
Yes. What would you like the new supervisor to achieve in the first three months?

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the interview.
examples: The hotel I work for now is quite small.
I'm also in charge of the weekend team.
I was responsible for training three new staff.
We had twice as many guests as usual.
spot.question: Where is the small word for in the first sentence? Which words come after in charge and after responsible? How much busier than usual was the hotel?
spot.answer: The hotel I work for: for goes at the end, and there is no which or that. In charge of and responsible for are fixed phrases, and after for you can use an -ing word: responsible for training. Twice as many guests as usual means two times the usual number.

rules.title: the company I worked for · responsible for, in charge of
rule: Keep the small word at the end: the company I worked for. Not: the company I worked.
You don't need who or which: the manager I reported to, the team I was part of.
responsible for + a noun or -ing: I was responsible for the stockroom, for ordering stock.
in charge of + a noun or -ing: She's in charge of a team of six.
Also: work for a company, work with customers, report to a manager.
rules.mistake: Not: I was responsible of the stockroom. Say: I was responsible for the stockroom.

rules.title: twice as many, by far the most
rule: Times: twice as many customers as last year, three times as fast.
Half: half as many complaints as before, half the time.
Numbers: sales went up by 20%, from 30 to 36 a day.
The biggest difference: by far the busiest, by far the most popular.
one of the most + plural: one of the most experienced drivers.
rules.mistake: Not: twice more customers than last year. Say: twice as many customers as last year.

practice.q: Mr Adeyemi is the manager I reported ___ .
practice.why: You report to a manager, so to goes at the end.

options: The team I was part of was great.
The team I was part was great.
The team of I was part was great.
practice.a: The team I was part of was great.
practice.why: The small word goes at the end: the team I was part of.

practice.q: She's in charge ___ a team of twelve.
I was responsible for ___ new staff.
practice.why: After for, use an -ing word: responsible for training.

practice.q: We served ___ customers as last year: 400, not 200.
practice.why: Twice as many + a noun + as: two times the number.

practice.q: This year we had ___ complaints as last year: 10, not 20.
practice.why: Half as many … as: 10 is half of 20.

practice.q: August was ___ the busiest month of the year.
practice.why: By far makes a superlative stronger: by far the busiest.

practice.q: She's one of the most experienced ___ in the company.
practice.why: One of the most + a plural noun.

practice.q: Our sales went up ___ 30% last year.
practice.why: Go up by + an amount: up by 30%.

yourTurn.prompt: An interviewer says to you: “Tell me about your last job.” Answer in four or five sentences. Say which company you worked for, what you were responsible for, and one result with a number.
starters: By the end, we had twice as …
yourTurn.model: The company I worked for was a small bakery in the city centre. I was responsible for the early shift, and I was in charge of two new assistants. I also ordered the flour and the other supplies. In my second year, we sold twice as many cakes as before, because we started taking orders online. It was by far the best job I've had.

text.title: A job application
text.body:
JOB APPLICATION
Position: Customer Service Team Leader (ref. CS-208)
Company: Linkway Mobile, Leeds office
Applicant: Amina Diallo

PROFILE
Customer service adviser with five years' experience in a busy call centre. I help about 60 customers a day, and last year my team had by far the best customer scores in the office. Fluent in English and French.

EXPERIENCE
2021 to now: Customer Service Adviser, Linkway Mobile
I answer phone and online questions about bills and contracts. I am in charge of training new advisers, and I trained 14 people last year.
2019 to 2021: Career break
I looked after my father when he was ill. This explains the gap in my CV.
2016 to 2019: Sales Assistant, Park Lane Shoes
I was responsible for the shop's online orders. We sold three times as many shoes online in 2018 as in 2016.

EDUCATION
2016: Degree in Business Studies

COVERING LETTER
Dear Mr Osei,
I am writing to apply for the role of Customer Service Team Leader. My experience is very relevant: I already train new advisers, and I deal with difficult calls every day. The company I work for now is growing fast, and I would now like to lead a team of my own. I am enthusiastic, patient and punctual. I have attached my CV.
I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours sincerely,
Amina Diallo

gist.q: What job is Amina applying for?
gist.why: The application is for the position of Customer Service Team Leader (ref. CS-208).

gist.q: Why does Amina want this job?
gist.a: She would like to lead a team.
wrong: She wants to move to Leeds.
gist.why: She writes: I would now like to lead a team of my own.

detail.q: What is Amina in charge of in her job now?
detail.why: She writes: I am in charge of training new advisers.

detail.q: Why is there a gap in her CV?
detail.a: She looked after her father when he was ill.
wrong: She was studying for a degree.
She lost her job at the shoe shop.
detail.why: 2019 to 2021: I looked after my father when he was ill.

detail.q: How did online sales change at Park Lane Shoes?
detail.a: They were three times higher in 2018 than in 2016.
wrong: They were half as high in 2018.
detail.why: She writes: We sold three times as many shoes online in 2018 as in 2016.

detail.q: Which languages does Amina speak well?
detail.why: Her profile says: Fluent in English and French.

items.meaning: A short document about your education, skills and work history. You send it when you apply for a job.
items.example: Please send your CV to the manager by Friday.

items.meaning: A short letter or email that you send with your CV. It says which job you want and why you are right for it.
items.example: Keep your covering letter short: one page is enough.

items.meaning: A short description of yourself at the top of your CV: who you are and what you can do.
items.example: Her profile says she has ten years' experience in sales.

items.meaning: A job or a position, and the things that the person in it has to do.
items.example: In my last role, I managed a small team.

items.meaning: Connected with the thing you are talking about or doing, and so useful.
items.example: Only put relevant experience on your CV.

items.meaning: Able to speak a language easily and well.
items.example: He's fluent in Arabic and English.

items.meaning: A qualification that you get when you finish a course at a university.
items.example: She has a degree in engineering.

items.meaning: The work of helping customers and dealing with their questions and problems.
items.example: I've worked in customer service for six years.

items.meaning: A period of time when something stops, for example a time in your life when you were not working.
items.example: There's a two-year gap in my CV because I was caring for my mother.

items.meaning: Very interested in something, and excited about doing it.
items.example: The new staff are enthusiastic and keen to learn.

items.meaning: To get a message, a letter or a phone call from someone.
items.example: Have you heard from the company about the job?

model.title: A CV profile and a covering message
model.body:
PROFILE
Experienced delivery driver with eight years on the road, the last four in charge of a team of six. Clean driving licence. Fluent in Polish and English.

COVERING MESSAGE
Dear Ms Chen,
I am writing to apply for the position of Delivery Supervisor (ref. DS-41), which I saw on your website. I have eight years' experience as a delivery driver, and for the last four years I have been in charge of the weekend team. Last year, our team had by far the fewest late deliveries in the company. I am punctual and flexible, and I am enthusiastic about this role. I have attached my CV.
I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours sincerely,
Tomasz Kowal

write.task: Write a short CV profile (two or three lines) and a covering message for a job you would like. Say which job you are applying for, what relevant experience you have, and one result with a number. It can be real or made up.
checklist: My profile says what I do and how long I have done it.
I named the job I am applying for.
I gave one result with a number: twice as many, by far the most …
I ended politely: I look forward to hearing from you.

card.title: The job interview
card.situation: You have an interview for a job that you would really like. It can be your real job or a new one. The interviewer will ask you three questions.
card.goal: Answer each question with a real example: the situation, what you did, and the result. At the end, ask the interviewer one good question.

phrases: In my last job, I was responsible for …
For example, last year we had …
Could you tell me what a typical week looks like?
I look forward to hearing from you.
prepare.notes: Write notes for three examples from your life: a time when you worked under pressure, a time when you worked in a team, and something you achieved. For each one, note the situation, what you did, and the result, with a number if you can. Then write one question for the interviewer.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is the interviewer. Answer three questions with real examples, then ask one question. Then listen to another learner and say one thing they did well.
doIt.wehel: You are the manager of a company, and you are interviewing me for a job. First ask me which job I am applying for. Then ask me three interview questions, one at a time. One of them must start: Tell me about a time when … After my answers, ask me: Do you have any questions for us? At the end, tell me one thing I did well and one thing to improve. Use simple English.

model.title: The interview
lines: Thanks for coming in. Please, take a seat.
So, tell me about your experience.
I've worked in a warehouse for four years. In my last job, I was responsible for checking all the deliveries.
Tell me about a time when you had to work under pressure.
Last December, we had twice as many orders as usual, and two people were ill. I made a new plan for the shifts, and we sent every order on time.
Well done. And what's your greatest strength?
Teamwork, I think. For example, when a new colleague joined, I helped her learn the system in two weeks instead of four.
Thank you. Do you have any questions for us?
Yes. What would you like the new person to achieve in the first three months?
Good question. We'd like the new stock system to be working by March.
Thank you. I look forward to hearing from you.
compare: Did you give a real example for each question, not only: I'm hard-working?
Did you say what the result was, with a number?
Did you use responsible for, in charge of or twice as many?
Did you ask a good question at the end?

canDo: I can talk about my experience: I was responsible for …, I was in charge of …
I can answer an interview question with a real example.
I can describe a result with numbers: twice as many, by far the most.
I can read a job application, and write a short CV profile and a covering message.
I can ask a good question at the end of an interview.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. What job does the person in the story do, or want to do? What do you think will happen?
reading.talk: What helped the person in the story at work? What job would you like to have in five years' time? Write three or four sentences, or tell Wehel about it.

quiz.q: That's the manager I used to report ___ .
quiz.why: You report to a manager, so to goes at the end.

quiz.q: She's in charge ___ the whole warehouse.
We had ___ orders as last year: 800, not 400.
quiz.why: 800 is two times 400: twice as many.

quiz.q: Our driver has left, so there's a ___ for a new driver.
quiz.why: A vacancy is a job that is available because nobody is doing it.

quiz.q: The interviewer says: Tell me about a time when you worked under pressure. Which answer is best?
options: Last May, two colleagues were ill, so I planned extra shifts and we finished on time.
I always work well under pressure.
I don't like pressure at work.
quiz.a: Last May, two colleagues were ill, so I planned extra shifts and we finished on time.
quiz.why: The question wants a real example: the situation, what you did and the result.

quiz.q: The interviewer asks: Do you have any questions for us? Which answer is best?
options: Yes. What would you like the new person to achieve in the first year?
No. What time can I go home?
quiz.a: Yes. What would you like the new person to achieve in the first year?
quiz.why: A question about the job shows that you are interested in it.
From a time in the past until now, with since: I have been working.
The passive with will: will be + past participle.

quiz.q: The manager told me ___ on Monday.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the interview in pairs. Then change the job and the examples: a nurse, a chef, a shop manager.
Day 2: results round. Each learner says one result from their working life with twice as many, half as many or by far the most, and the class asks one question about it.
Day 3: the task. You are the interviewer. Each learner answers three questions with real examples, then asks you one question. The class notes one good example each time.
Day 4: talk about the book and answer questions. Then learners read their CV profiles aloud, and the class says which candidate they would call, and why.
